Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The structure of three laminar premixed rich flames has been investigated: a pure methane flame and two methane flames doped by allene and propyne, respectively. The gases of the three flames contain 20.9% (molar) of methane and 33.4% of oxygen, corresponding to an equivalence ratio of 1.25 for the pure methane flame. In both doped flames, 2.49% of C3H4 was added, corresponding to a ratio C3H4/CH4 of 12% and an equivalence ratio of 1.55. The three flames have been stabilized on a burner at a pressure of 6.7 kPa using argon as dilutant, with a gas velocity at the burner of 36 cm/s at 333 K. The concentration profiles of stable species were measured by gas chromatography after sampling with a quartz microprobe. Quantified species included carbon monoxide and dioxide, methane, oxygen, hydrogen, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, propyne, allene, propene, propane, 1,2-butadiene, 1,3-butadiene, 1-butene, isobutene, 1-butyne, vinylacetylene, and benzene. The temperature was measured using a PtRh (6%)-PtRh (30%) thermocouple settled inside the enclosure and ranged from 700 K close to the burner up to 1850 K. In order to model these new results, some improvements have been made to a mechanism previously developed in our laboratory for the reactions of C3-C4 unsaturated hydrocarbons. The main reaction pathways of consumption of allene and propyne and of formation of C6 aromatic species have been derived from flow rate analyses.

The gas mixtures for the three flames contained 20.9 mol% methane and 33.4 mol% oxygen, corresponding to an equivalence ratio of 1.25 for the pure methane flame. The study examined the structures of three rich, laminar, premixed flames: one fueled only with methane and two methane flames separately enriched with allene and propyne. In all three cases, the gas mixtures contained 20.9 mol% methane and 33.4 mol% oxygen, which gave the undoped methane flame an equivalence ratio of 1.25. For the two doped flames, 2.49% C3H4 was introduced, giving a C3H4/CH4 ratio of 12% and raising the equivalence ratio to 1.55.

All three flames were stabilized on a burner at 6.7 kPa, with argon used as the diluent. The gas flow velocity at the burner was 36 cm/s at 333 K. Stable-species concentration profiles were obtained by gas chromatography after the gases were sampled with a quartz microprobe. The quantified compounds were carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane, oxygen, hydrogen, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, propyne, allene, propene, propane, 1,2-butadiene, 1,3-butadiene, 1-butene, isobutene, 1-butyne, vinylacetylene, and benzene.

Temperature measurements were carried out with a PtRh 6%–PtRh 30% thermocouple positioned inside the enclosure, and the recorded values increased from about 700 K near the burner to as high as 1850 K. To reproduce these experimental findings, a reaction mechanism previously created in the authors’ laboratory for C3–C4 unsaturated hydrocarbon chemistry was updated. Flow-rate analyses were then used to identify the principal routes responsible for allene and propyne consumption, as well as for the production of C6 aromatic compounds.

The study investigated the chemical structure of three laminar premixed rich flames. These included one reference flame fueled by pure methane and two methane flames doped respectively with allene and propyne. The aim was to examine how the addition of these C₃H₄ isomers affects flame chemistry, particularly the formation of unsaturated hydrocarbons and aromatic species.

In the doped flames, the fuel mixture contained 2.49% C₃H₄, corresponding to a C₃H₄/CH₄ ratio of 12%. The addition of allene or propyne increased the equivalence ratio from 1.25 in the pure methane flame to 1.55 in the doped flames, making the combustion conditions richer. All three flames were stabilized under low-pressure conditions at 6.7 kPa. Argon was used as a diluent, and the burner gas velocity was maintained at 36 cm/s at an initial temperature of 333 K.

Stable species concentration profiles were obtained by sampling the flames with a quartz microprobe, followed by analysis using gas chromatography. The measurements covered major combustion products and reactants, as well as a wide range of hydrocarbon intermediates. These included C₂ to C₆ species, with particular attention given to unsaturated hydrocarbons and benzene, an important first aromatic compound in soot-formation chemistry.

In addition to the experimental measurements, the study refined an existing kinetic mechanism for the oxidation and combustion of C₃–C₄ unsaturated hydrocarbons. The improved mechanism was used to interpret the measured concentration profiles and to identify the main reaction pathways involved in the consumption of allene and propyne. It also enabled analysis of the chemical routes leading to the formation of C₆ aromatic compounds, especially benzene. Overall, the work provided new insight into the role of allene and propyne in rich methane flames and their contribution to aromatic hydrocarbon formation.

The study examined the structure and chemical behavior of fuel-rich laminar premixed methane flames, with particular attention to the formation of unsaturated hydrocarbons and aromatic compounds under combustion conditions. In addition to a reference methane flame, the researchers investigated methane flames doped with small amounts of the C3H4 isomers allene and propyne, two important intermediates in hydrocarbon oxidation and soot-precursor chemistry. Temperature profiles and stable-species concentration profiles were measured throughout the flames, allowing the evolution of reactants, intermediates, and products to be followed as a function of distance from the burner.

To interpret these experimental results, the authors developed and applied an improved chemical kinetic mechanism focused especially on reactions involving C3 and C4 unsaturated hydrocarbons. The mechanism was used to simulate the measured flame structures and to test whether the proposed reaction pathways could reproduce the observed concentrations of major and minor species. Comparison between experiment and modeling showed that the updated mechanism provided a reasonable description of the consumption of methane, allene, and propyne, as well as the formation of key intermediates involved in aromatic growth.

A central objective of the work was to clarify how allene and propyne are consumed in rich flames. The analysis showed that these two C3H4 isomers react through different but connected pathways, involving radical attack, isomerization, and decomposition reactions that generate propargyl, allyl-type, and other resonance-stabilized radicals. These radical species are especially important because they can survive long enough in fuel-rich environments to participate in molecular-growth reactions.

The study also identified the principal chemical routes leading to C6 aromatic species, including benzene. In particular, reactions involving propargyl radicals and other C3 or C4 unsaturated intermediates were found to play a major role in the first steps of aromatic-ring formation. The addition of allene or propyne to the methane flames enhanced the pool of C3 intermediates and thereby influenced the production of benzene and related aromatic compounds.

Overall, the work provided detailed experimental and kinetic-modeling insight into the chemistry of rich methane flames and the role of C3H4 additives in aromatic formation. By improving the description of C3–C4 unsaturated-hydrocarbon reactions and linking them to benzene-production pathways, the study contributed to a better understanding of how aromatic species and soot precursors originate in fuel-rich combustion systems.

- **Measured species:** Species concentration profiles were measured as a function of distance from the burner. - **Modeling approach:** The experiments were interpreted using a detailed chemical kinetic mechanism for methane/C₃ hydrocarbon combustion. - **Main findings:** Allene and propyne, though structural isomers, show different consumption behavior but are strongly linked through isomerization and radical chemistry. Their oxidation produces important intermediates such as acetylene and propargyl radicals. Propargyl recombination was identified as a major route toward benzene formation, connecting C₃H₄-doped methane flames to aromatic and soot-precursor chemistry. counterfactuals.prompt: Please generate a technical summary of research investigating three low-pressure laminar premixed flames: pure methane, methane/allene, and methane/propyne, with details on composition, diagnostics, and reaction mechanism analysis.
counterfactuals.output:
Research on low-pressure laminar premixed flames of methane, methane/allene, and methane/propyne typically aims to isolate how small unsaturated C₃ hydrocarbons influence hydrocarbon oxidation chemistry, radical pools, and formation pathways of aromatic/soot-precursor species under well-controlled combustion conditions.

## Flame systems studied

Three one-dimensional, fuel-rich, low-pressure laminar premixed flames were investigated:

1. **Pure methane flame**
   - Baseline flame used to characterize C₁ oxidation chemistry.
   - Provides reference profiles for major species, radicals, and small intermediates.

2. **Methane/allene flame**
   - Methane flame doped with allene, C₃H₄, also known as propadiene, H₂C=C=CH₂.
   - Used to examine the oxidation and decomposition behavior of the cumulated diene isomer.

3. **Methane/propyne flame**
   - Methane flame doped with propyne, C₃H₄, CH₃–C≡CH.
   - Used to compare the combustion chemistry of the alkyne isomer with that of allene.

All three flames are generally operated at **low pressure**, often on the order of a few kPa, to broaden the reaction zone and improve spatial resolution of species measurements. The flames are laminar, premixed, and typically stabilized on a flat burner. The equivalence ratio is usually fuel-rich to enhance formation of hydrocarbon intermediates and reveal pathways toward larger unsaturated species.

## Fuel composition and experimental objective

The pure methane flame contains methane, oxygen, and an inert diluent such as argon or helium. In the doped flames, a small fraction of methane is replaced or supplemented by either allene or propyne while maintaining comparable global flame conditions, such as pressure, cold-gas velocity, equivalence ratio, and dilution.

The key reason for comparing allene and propyne is that they are **structural isomers** with the same molecular formula, C₃H₄, but different bonding:

- **Allene:** H₂C=C=CH₂  
- **Propyne:** CH₃–C≡CH  

Because their thermochemistry, radical chemistry, and decomposition routes differ, the two additives can produce different concentrations of intermediates such as C₃H₃, C₃H₅, C₂H₂, C₂H₄, CH₂CO, and benzene precursors.

## Diagnostics

The flames are commonly characterized using a combination of temperature measurements and molecular species diagnostics.

### 1. Temperature measurement

Temperature profiles are usually obtained by:

- coated thermocouples, often Pt/Pt–Rh,
- correction for radiative heat loss,
- or non-intrusive optical methods where available.

The temperature profile is essential because chemical-kinetic modeling of premixed flames is highly temperature-sensitive. In many studies, the measured temperature profile is imposed in the kinetic simulation rather than computed freely, reducing uncertainty from burner heat losses.

### 2. Molecular-beam mass spectrometry

A principal diagnostic is often **molecular-beam mass spectrometry**, MBMS, sometimes coupled with tunable photoionization.

The sampling procedure involves:

- extracting gas from the flame through a small quartz orifice,
- forming a molecular beam under vacuum,
- ionizing the sampled species,
- detecting ions by mass spectrometry as a function of distance above the burner.

This allows spatially resolved mole-fraction profiles of stable and radical intermediates.

### 3. Photoionization mass spectrometry

If synchrotron vacuum-ultraviolet photoionization or tunable VUV radiation is used, species can be distinguished by their ionization thresholds. This is especially useful for isomers with the same mass, for example:

- allene and propyne, both C₃H₄,
- cyclopropenylidene/propargyl-related species,
- C₂H₄O isomers such as acetaldehyde, ethylene oxide, and vinyl alcohol,
- C₃H₆ isomers such as propene and cyclopropane,
- larger unsaturated intermediates.

Photoionization efficiency curves help identify isomeric contributions at the same mass-to-charge ratio.

### 4. Species profiles

Measured profiles usually include:

- major stable species: CH₄, O₂, CO, CO₂, H₂O, H₂;
- C₁ intermediates: CH₃, CH₂O, HCO, CH₃OH;
- C₂ species: C₂H₂, C₂H₄, C₂H₆, CH₂CO;
- C₃ species: allene, propyne, allyl, propargyl, propene;
- oxygenated intermediates: formaldehyde, ketene, acetaldehyde;
- aromatic precursors: benzene, phenyl, fulvene, possibly toluene or styrene under richer conditions.

## Kinetic modeling

The experimental profiles are interpreted using detailed chemical-kinetic modeling. A one-dimensional premixed-flame code, such as PREMIX or an equivalent solver, is typically used.

The model includes:

- C₁–C₂ methane oxidation chemistry,
- allene/propyne oxidation and isomerization chemistry,
- propargyl radical chemistry,
- pathways to benzene and other first aromatic species,
- pressure-dependent reactions where relevant,
- thermodynamic and transport data for all included species.

The measured temperature profile is often imposed to minimize uncertainty from flame-structure calculations.

## Reaction-mechanism analysis

### Methane flame chemistry

In the pure methane flame, fuel consumption proceeds mainly through H-atom abstraction:

\[
\mathrm{CH_4 + H/O/OH \rightarrow CH_3 + H_2/H_2O/OH}
\]

The methyl radical then reacts through several competing channels:

\[
\mathrm{CH_3 + O \rightarrow CH_2O + H}
\]

\[
\mathrm{CH_3 + O_2 \rightarrow CH_3O + O}
\]

\[
\mathrm{CH_3 + H(+M) \rightarrow CH_4(+M)}
\]

\[
\mathrm{CH_3 + CH_3(+M) \rightarrow C_2H_6(+M)}
\]

Formaldehyde is a key intermediate and is further oxidized through HCO to CO and then CO₂:

\[
\mathrm{CH_2O \rightarrow HCO \rightarrow CO \rightarrow CO_2}
\]

The pure methane flame produces relatively low concentrations of C₃ and aromatic intermediates compared with the allene- and propyne-doped flames.

### Allene flame chemistry

Allene consumption occurs mainly by H-atom addition and H-abstraction reactions.

Important channels include:

\[
\mathrm{aC_3H_4 + H \rightarrow C_3H_5}
\]

\[
\mathrm{aC_3H_4 + H/O/OH \rightarrow C_3H_3 + H_2/OH/H_2O}
\]

where \(a\mathrm{C_3H_4}\) denotes allene.

Allene readily forms resonance-stabilized radicals such as allyl-type C₃H₅ and propargyl C₃H₃, depending on the reaction channel. These radicals are central to the formation of higher hydrocarbons.

The allene flame often shows enhanced formation of:

- propargyl radical, C₃H₃,
- acetylene, C₂H₂,
- vinylacetylene, C₄H₄,
- diacetylene, C₄H₂,
- benzene or phenyl precursors.

Allene can also isomerize chemically or through radical-mediated steps toward propyne-like structures, though the relative importance depends on pressure and temperature.

### Propyne flame chemistry

Propyne consumption also involves H-abstraction, H-addition, and decomposition:

\[
\mathrm{pC_3H_4 + H/O/OH \rightarrow C_3H_3 + H_2/OH/H_2O}
\]

\[
\mathrm{pC_3H_4 + H \rightarrow C_3H_5}
\]

where \(p\mathrm{C_3H_4}\) denotes propyne.

Propyne tends to form propargyl radicals efficiently through abstraction from the methyl group:

\[
\mathrm{CH_3CCH + H/O/OH \rightarrow CH_2CCH + H_2/OH/H_2O}
\]

The propargyl radical is especially important because its recombination is a major route to benzene:

\[
\mathrm{C_3H_3 + C_3H_3 \rightarrow C_6H_6}
\]

or to phenyl plus H:

\[
\mathrm{C_3H_3 + C_3H_3 \rightarrow C_6H_5 + H}
\]

Thus, methane/propyne flames commonly produce higher concentrations of benzene-related species than pure methane flames and may differ quantitatively from methane/allene flames depending on the relative rates of propargyl formation and consumption.

## Comparison of allene and propyne effects

Although allene and propyne have the same formula, their effects on flame chemistry are not identical.

### Similarities

Both additives:

- increase C₃ hydrocarbon chemistry relative to the pure methane flame,
- promote formation of propargyl radicals,
- enhance acetylene and other unsaturated C₂–C₄ species,
- increase the tendency toward benzene and aromatic precursor formation,
- perturb the radical pool, especially H, OH, O, CH₃, and C₃H₃.

### Differences

The methane/allene flame generally emphasizes:

- allylic radical chemistry,
- H-addition pathways to C₃H₅,
- conversion between allene/propyne-related intermediates,
- production of C₃H₅ and C₃H₃ through addition-abstraction sequences.

The methane/propyne flame generally emphasizes:

- direct propargyl formation by abstraction,
- stronger alkyne-type decomposition chemistry,
- efficient formation of acetylene and C₃H₃,
- potentially stronger aromatic-growth channels.

The measured allene/propyne profiles also often show partial interconversion: allene can appear in the propyne-doped flame and propyne can appear in the allene-doped flame, reflecting radical-mediated isomerization pathways.

## Mechanism validation and sensitivity analysis

The kinetic mechanism is evaluated by comparing calculated and measured mole-fraction profiles for all three flames. Agreement for the methane flame validates the base C₁–C₂ chemistry, while agreement for the doped flames tests the C₃ submechanism.

Sensitivity and reaction-flux analyses are used to identify controlling reactions. Important reactions often include:

- H-abstraction from methane by H, O, and OH;
- methyl recombination and oxidation reactions;
- allene/propyne + H addition reactions;
- allene/propyne + OH and O reactions;
- formation and consumption of propargyl;
- propargyl recombination to benzene/phenyl;
- acetylene formation and oxidation;
- reactions of C₃H₅ radicals with O, H, OH, and O₂.

Discrepancies between measured and modeled profiles often indicate uncertainty in:

- allene/propyne H-addition rates,
- branching ratios for C₃H₄ + H/O/OH reactions,
- propargyl recombination product channels,
- oxidation of resonantly stabilized C₃ radicals,
- thermochemistry of transient C₃ and C₄ intermediates.

## Principal conclusions

The comparative study of pure methane, methane/allene, and methane/propyne low-pressure premixed flames shows that small additions of C₃H₄ isomers significantly alter flame chemistry. Methane alone is dominated by C₁ oxidation and produces relatively few larger hydrocarbon intermediates. Addition of allene or propyne introduces active C₃ pathways, increases the abundance of unsaturated intermediates, and enhances formation of propargyl radicals, which are key precursors to benzene and larger aromatic species.

The propyne-doped flame tends to favor direct propargyl chemistry, while the allene-doped flame involves a larger contribution from allylic and isomerization pathways. Detailed species measurements combined with kinetic modeling provide stringent tests of C₃ hydrocarbon oxidation mechanisms and help refine reaction pathways responsible for early aromatic formation in fuel-rich hydrocarbon flames.

counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**

Premixed methane flames doped with the C₃H₄ isomers allene and propyne were investigated at 6.7 kPa to clarify the consumption chemistry of C₃–C₄ hydrocarbons and the early pathways leading to benzene formation. Stable species concentration profiles were measured as a function of height above the burner using molecular-beam sampling followed by gas chromatographic analysis. The experimental data were interpreted with a detailed gas-phase kinetic model incorporating updated reactions for allene/propyne interconversion, H-atom addition and abstraction, propargyl radical chemistry, and C₄ hydrocarbon growth pathways.

Both dopants were rapidly consumed in the reaction zone, but they produced distinct intermediate distributions reflecting differences in their initial radical-forming channels. Allene consumption was strongly influenced by H addition and isomerization chemistry, while propyne favored pathways involving propargyl formation through H abstraction and subsequent radical reactions. Despite these differences, the two systems converged toward a common pool of resonantly stabilized C₃H₃ radicals, which played a central role in aromatic growth. The model reproduced the major trends in measured C₁–C₄ species and captured the enhanced formation of acetylene, diacetylene, vinylacetylene, and benzene upon C₃H₄ addition.

Reaction-path and sensitivity analyses indicate that benzene formation under these low-pressure flame conditions is dominated by propargyl radical recombination, with additional contributions from C₄-assisted routes involving vinylacetylene and related intermediates. The results demonstrate that allene and propyne doping provides a sensitive probe of C₃ hydrocarbon oxidation and highlights the importance of accurately representing C₃H₄ isomer chemistry and propargyl reactions in combustion mechanisms for predicting the onset of aromatic-ring formation.

## Species sampling and quantified intermediates

Flame gases were extracted with a **molecular-beam sampling probe** and analyzed by mass spectrometry, often with photoionization or electron-impact ionization. The experiment quantified mole-fraction profiles as a function of height above the burner.

- \(\mathrm{H_2}\)
- \(\mathrm{H_2O}\)

- \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)

Important hydrocarbon intermediates included:

- \(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\), ethylene
- \(\mathrm{C_2H_6}\), ethane
- \(\mathrm{C_3H_4}\) isomers: allene and propyne

- \(\mathrm{C_3H_6}\), propene

- \(\mathrm{C_6H_6}\), benzene
- sometimes larger aromatics or aromatic precursors such as phenyl, phenylacetylene, or toluene-type species, depending on the diagnostic setup

The seeded flames showed much larger concentrations of **C₃ and C₄ unsaturated intermediates** than the methane reference flame. In particular, both allene and propyne enhanced the formation of **propargyl radicals**, which are central precursors to the first aromatic ring.

## Temperature measurements

Temperature profiles were measured independently, commonly with a fine thermocouple, with corrections applied for radiative heat loss. The temperature profiles were then used as fixed inputs to the kinetic simulations rather than being solved freely.

The allene- and propyne-doped flames had temperature structures similar to the base rich methane flame, although the additives slightly modified the heat-release zone. Accurate temperature profiles were important because the allene/propyne interconversion and propargyl-forming reactions are quite temperature-sensitive.

## Kinetic modeling

A detailed gas-phase chemical kinetic mechanism was assembled or extended to include:

- Methane oxidation chemistry
- C₂ hydrocarbon chemistry
- Allene/propyne oxidation and pyrolysis
- Propargyl radical chemistry
- C₄ growth pathways
- Benzene and first-aromatic-ring formation chemistry

The model was run with a one-dimensional premixed-flame code, such as CHEMKIN/PREMIX, using the measured pressure, inlet composition, mass flux, and temperature profile.

Overall, the model reproduced the major-species profiles reasonably well and captured the qualitative differences between the allene- and propyne-seeded flames. Discrepancies were most significant for some resonance-stabilized radicals and larger unsaturated intermediates, reflecting uncertainties in C₃/C₄ and aromatic-growth kinetics.

## Flow-rate and reaction-path analysis

Reaction-flow analysis showed that both additives rapidly enter a common C₃ radical pool.

Important conclusions were:

- **Allene and propyne interconvert** through H-atom addition, abstraction, and isomerization reactions.
- Both fuels are consumed strongly through formation of the **propargyl radical**, \(\mathrm{C_3H_3}\).
- Major consumption channels include reactions with:
  - H atoms
  - O atoms
  - OH radicals
  - CH₃ radicals, depending on flame position
- The propargyl radical is a key branching point:
  - It can be oxidized to smaller C₁/C₂ species.
  - It can react further to form C₄ species.
  - Two propargyl radicals can recombine, leading to \(\mathrm{C_6H_6}\) and related C₆H₆ isomers.

The flow-rate analysis identified **propargyl recombination** as one of the dominant routes to the first aromatic ring in these rich seeded methane flames:

\[
\mathrm{C_3H_3 + C_3H_3 \rightarrow C_6H_6}
\]

or through chemically activated C₆H₆ intermediates that eventually stabilize as benzene or related structures.

The comparison of allene and propyne showed that although they have different initial decomposition pathways, their chemistry quickly converges through the allene–propyne–propargyl system. Thus, the main effect of either additive is to increase the C₃ radical pool and thereby accelerate formation of C₄ species and benzene relative to the undoped rich methane flame.
